questions.title: Why Gamma Forces Constant Rehedging
questions.prompt: A dealer delta-hedges a short call position at the open. By midday, after the stock has moved $4, the hedge is meaningfully off. Explain precisely why, using gamma, and describe what 'high gamma' means for how often a desk has to rebalance.
questions.modelAnswer: Gamma is the second derivative of option value with respect to the underlying — the rate of change of delta itself as the stock moves. Delta-hedging only neutralizes a position for an instantaneous, small move; as the stock actually moves $4, delta shifts by an amount approximately equal to gamma times that move, so the stock hedge sized for the original delta is no longer correct. Gamma is always positive for long options and identical for calls and puts at the same strike and expiration, peaking for at-the-money options near expiration. A high-gamma position (short-dated, near-the-money options) needs frequent rebalancing because delta is changing quickly; a low-gamma position (deep in/out-of-the-money, longer-dated) can go longer between rehedges without the hedge drifting meaningfully out of balance.
questions.professionalAnswer: Gamma is sometimes described as 'how often you'll need to retrade your hedge,' and that framing is exactly right here. A $4 move on a high-gamma book means delta has shifted enough that the morning's hedge is stale by midday — this isn't a mistake, it's the expected cost of holding gamma, and it's exactly why short-dated, near-the-money options desks rehedge far more often than a desk holding longer-dated, less convex positions.
questions.example: A call with gamma of 0.03 per $1 move will see its delta shift by roughly 0.03 x 4 = 0.12 after a $4 stock move — on 100 contracts covering 10,000 shares of notional, that's a meaningful 1,200-share hedge gap that needs to be closed.
commonMistakes: Treating the stale hedge as a sign of an error rather than the expected consequence of gamma
Forgetting that gamma is identical for calls and puts at the same strike/expiration
Not connecting gamma's magnitude (ATM, short-dated vs. deep ITM/OTM, long-dated) to rehedging frequency
Confusing gamma with vega (volatility sensitivity)
keyPoints: Gamma = rate of change of delta with respect to the underlying
Delta-hedging is only accurate for small, instantaneous moves
Gamma is positive for long options, identical for calls/puts at the same strike/expiry
High gamma (ATM, short-dated) requires frequent rebalancing; low gamma allows less frequent rebalancing

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains gamma as the rate of change of delta
Explains why the $4 move breaks the original hedge
Connects gamma magnitude to rehedging frequency across different option profiles

questions.title: Reading the Volatility Skew
questions.prompt: On an equity index, one-month at-the-money implied volatility is 16%, while the one-month put struck 10% out-of-the-money implies 22%. If Black-Scholes assumed constant volatility, every strike would show the same number. What does this six-point gap actually tell you, and why does it exist?
questions.modelAnswer: This is the volatility skew: for equity index options, implied volatility is typically higher for low strikes (out-of-the-money puts) and lower for high strikes, because investors buy downside puts to hedge against crashes, bidding up their price and therefore their implied volatility relative to what constant-volatility Black-Scholes would predict. The skew isn't a market inefficiency to be arbitraged away — it's direct, observable evidence that real stock returns don't follow the lognormal, constant-volatility process Black-Scholes assumes: returns have fatter tails than lognormal predicts, and volatility itself clusters and changes over time rather than sitting at one constant level. Practitioners respond by pricing each option using the implied volatility the market assigns to that specific strike and expiration (the volatility surface) rather than one flat number for every strike.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd read that six-point gap as the market explicitly pricing crash insurance demand into downside puts, not as noise or a mispricing to trade against. It's also a direct, quotable piece of evidence that Black-Scholes's constant-volatility assumption is wrong in practice — fat tails are real, and the skew is the market's own fingerprint of that fact.
questions.example: If Black-Scholes's assumptions held exactly, the entire implied-volatility curve at a fixed expiration would be flat at one number regardless of strike; a skew where OTM puts show materially higher IV than ATM options is the market openly disagreeing with that assumption.
commonMistakes: Treating the skew as a pricing error to be arbitraged rather than a reflection of real tail risk and hedging demand
Confusing skew (variation by strike) with term structure (variation by expiration)
Not connecting the skew to fat tails and the breakdown of the lognormal assumption
Assuming the smile/skew is identical across all asset classes (equity index skew vs. FX smile have different typical shapes and explanations)
keyPoints: Skew: IV higher for low (OTM put) strikes, lower for high strikes, in equity index options
Driven by demand for downside crash protection, bidding up low-strike IV
Reflects real fat tails and non-constant volatility, which Black-Scholes doesn't assume
Practitioners price per-strike/expiration using the volatility surface, not one flat sigma

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly defines the skew and its typical shape for equity index options
Explains the demand-for-protection mechanism driving it
Connects the skew to the breakdown of Black-Scholes's constant-volatility assumption

questions.title: VaR's Blind Spot, and Why ES Fixes It
questions.prompt: Two portfolios have an identical 99% VaR. One loses only slightly more than the VaR threshold on its worst days; the other loses catastrophically more. Why does VaR alone fail to distinguish these two cases, and how does Expected Shortfall fix it?
questions.modelAnswer: VaR reports only the threshold a loss is unlikely to cross — it says nothing about how bad things get once that threshold is actually crossed, which is exactly why two portfolios with identical VaR can have wildly different tail severity. Expected Shortfall (ES), also called Conditional VaR, answers a different question: given that the loss exceeds the VaR threshold, what is the average loss in that tail? Where VaR marks a cutoff point, ES averages the severity of everything beyond it, directly addressing VaR's tail-blindness. ES is also a coherent risk measure (satisfying sub-additivity, which VaR does not guarantee in general), which is a major reason the Basel Committee's FRTB moved minimum trading-book capital requirements from VaR toward a 97.5% Expected Shortfall measure.
questions.professionalAnswer: VaR tells you where the common range of bad days ends; it's silent on what 'worse than that' actually looks like. ES fixes that specifically by averaging everything past the cutoff instead of just marking where the cutoff is — which is exactly the number I'd want if I were trying to compare two portfolios that look identical on VaR alone but could have very different real tail risk.
questions.example: Two portfolios both have a 99% VaR of 2%, but Portfolio A's worst 1% of days average a 2.3% loss while Portfolio B's worst 1% of days average an 8% loss — VaR alone can't distinguish them, but Expected Shortfall immediately reveals Portfolio B is far riskier in the tail.
commonMistakes: Treating VaR and Expected Shortfall as interchangeable risk numbers
Not explaining what 'tail-blindness' specifically means for VaR
Missing the sub-additivity/coherence distinction between the two measures
Not mentioning the real-world regulatory shift (FRTB) toward Expected Shortfall
keyPoints: VaR marks a loss threshold; it says nothing about severity beyond that threshold
Expected Shortfall averages the loss conditional on exceeding the VaR threshold
ES is a coherent risk measure (sub-additive); VaR is not guaranteed to be
Regulators (Basel FRTB) moved capital requirements toward 97.5% Expected Shortfall

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains VaR's tail-blindness
Correctly explains how Expected Shortfall addresses it
Mentions coherence/sub-additivity or the regulatory shift as supporting context

questions.title: Exploiting a Put-Call Parity Violation
questions.prompt: S=$50, K=$50, r=5% continuous, T=1 year, and the call trades at $4.50. The put is quoted at $3.00 in the market. Is parity violated, and if so, what trade locks in a riskless profit?
questions.code:
C - P = S - K*e^(-rT)
Fair P = C - S + K*e^(-rT)
questions.modelAnswer: Fair put price = C - S + K*e^(-rT) = 4.50 - 50 + 50*e^(-0.05) = 4.50 - 50 + 47.56 = $2.06. The market is quoting the put at $3.00, which is about $0.94 overpriced relative to parity. To exploit this: sell the overpriced put, buy the call, short the stock, and lend the proceeds at the risk-free rate. At expiration, this position's payoffs cancel out exactly regardless of where the stock ends up, locking in the $0.94 mispricing today as riskless profit — and this is exactly the kind of activity that competes the mispricing away almost instantly in real markets.
questions.professionalAnswer: The fair put price comes straight out of C - P = S - Ke^(-rT) rearranged for P — here that's $2.06. The actual put is quoted a full $0.94 above that, so the trade is: sell the expensive put, buy the cheap synthetic equivalent (long call, short stock, lend the strike's present value), and the payoff is identical in every future state, which is the entire definition of a riskless arbitrage.
questions.example: pv_K = 50 * e^(-0.05) ≈ 47.56; fair P = 4.50 - 50 + 47.56 = 2.06; mispricing = 3.00 - 2.06 = 0.94 captured risklessly today.
commonMistakes: Computing the fair put price with the wrong sign or forgetting to discount the strike
Getting the direction of the arbitrage trade backward (buying the overpriced side instead of selling it)
Not recognizing that the trade must be riskless at every future outcome, not just favorable on average
Forgetting to include the stock leg (shorting the stock) in the replicating trade
keyPoints: Fair put price: P = C - S + K*e^(-rT) = $2.06
The market put at $3.00 is overpriced relative to parity by about $0.94
Arbitrage trade: sell the put, buy the call, short the stock, lend K*e^(-rT)
The position's payoff is identical across all future outcomes, locking in the mispricing risklessly

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly computes the fair put price ($2.06)
Correctly identifies the direction and size of the mispricing
Correctly describes the full arbitrage trade (all four legs)

questions.title: Reading a GARCH(1,1) Fit
questions.prompt: A GARCH(1,1) model fit to daily equity returns comes back with alpha=0.08 and beta=0.90. What does that specific combination tell you about how this market's volatility behaves, and why is alpha+beta<1 a condition you need to check?
questions.modelAnswer: Alpha measures how strongly a fresh shock moves conditional variance, and beta measures persistence — how much of yesterday's variance carries into today. Alpha=0.08 and beta=0.90 describes a market where a single day's shock has a modest immediate effect on variance, but volatility is highly persistent: once volatility rises, it decays slowly, so a turbulent week can leave the market jumpy for a long stretch afterward. Alpha+beta<1 (here, 0.98<1) is required for the process to be covariance stationary with a well-defined long-run average variance — if alpha+beta were at or above 1, shocks to variance would never fully decay, and the model would imply volatility has no stable long-run level to revert to, which would make any multi-step forecast based on mean-reversion invalid.
questions.professionalAnswer: Alpha+beta at 0.98 is a classic, highly persistent real-equity-data fit — it says once volatility spikes, it's going to stay elevated for a while, not snap back the next day. Checking alpha+beta<1 isn't a formality; it's the condition that guarantees the model's forecasts actually mean-revert toward a stable long-run variance instead of exploding or staying permanently elevated.
questions.example: With alpha+beta=0.98, a multi-step-ahead GARCH forecast will flatten out toward the long-run unconditional variance only slowly, reflecting that a shock today still meaningfully influences the variance forecast many days out.
commonMistakes: Confusing alpha (shock sensitivity) and beta (persistence) with each other
Not explaining why alpha+beta<1 matters for stationarity
Treating a high alpha+beta sum as a model error rather than a genuine feature of persistent real equity volatility
Missing that this combination implies slow mean-reversion in multi-step forecasts
keyPoints: Alpha: sensitivity of variance to a fresh shock
Beta: persistence of past variance into today
alpha+beta<1 required for covariance stationarity / a well-defined long-run variance
High beta (e.g., 0.90) implies slow-decaying, highly persistent volatility shocks

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly distinguishes alpha and beta
Correctly interprets the specific alpha/beta combination given
Correctly explains the role of the alpha+beta<1 stationarity condition

questions.title: Correlation Is Not Cointegration
questions.prompt: Two stocks show a 0.92 correlation over the last three years. A junior researcher wants to immediately build a pairs trade on them. What's missing from that justification, and what test should actually be run first?
questions.modelAnswer: High correlation alone doesn't justify a pairs trade — two prices can be highly correlated over a sample and still wander apart forever, for instance if both simply trended up during the same bull market for unrelated reasons. What a pairs trade actually needs is cointegration: a stable, mean-reverting long-run relationship between the two series, even if each series individually behaves like a random walk. The standard test is the Engle-Granger two-step procedure — regress one price on the other to estimate the hedge ratio, then test whether the regression's residual (the spread) is itself stationary, typically using an Augmented Dickey-Fuller test. A high correlation with no cointegration is exactly the setup that produces a pairs trade that looks appealing on paper and then simply doesn't converge.
questions.professionalAnswer: 0.92 correlation tells you almost nothing on its own about whether this spread will actually mean-revert — that's the trap. I'd run Engle-Granger before committing to anything: regress one on the other, test the residual for stationarity with an ADF test, and only trust the pair if that residual genuinely looks mean-reverting, not just because the raw correlation number looks impressive.
questions.example: Two unrelated growth stocks that both rallied through a multi-year bull market could show a 0.92 correlation purely from both trending in the same direction, with no actual mean-reverting relationship between their prices at all — exactly the setup an Engle-Granger test would correctly flag as non-cointegrated.
commonMistakes: Treating high correlation as sufficient evidence for a pairs trade
Not naming a specific test (Engle-Granger / ADF) to check cointegration
Confusing the hedge ratio regression step with the stationarity test step
Missing that the spread (residual), not the raw prices, is what needs to be tested for stationarity
keyPoints: Correlation does not imply cointegration
Cointegration requires a stable, mean-reverting long-run relationship
Engle-Granger: regress to get the hedge ratio, then ADF-test the residual (spread) for stationarity
High correlation with no cointegration is a common, costly trap in pairs trading

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains why correlation alone is insufficient
Correctly names cointegration as the required property
Correctly describes the Engle-Granger / ADF testing procedure

questions.title: The Three Priced-In Risks Behind a Spread, Revisited
questions.prompt: Explain each of order-processing cost, inventory risk, and adverse selection in enough depth to say specifically which one dominates for a highly liquid large-cap stock versus a thinly traded small-cap right before earnings.
questions.modelAnswer: Order-processing cost is the pure operational cost of handling a trade (exchange fees, technology) and is largely independent of the specific stock or timing. Inventory risk is the cost of holding a position between trades — it rises with volatility, since a more volatile stock is more likely to move against the market maker before they can offload the position. Adverse selection is the risk of trading against a better-informed counterparty — it rises sharply whenever informed trading is more likely, such as right before an earnings release. For a highly liquid large-cap stock in calm conditions, order-processing cost tends to dominate the (very tight) spread, since inventory and information risk are both low. For a thinly traded small-cap right before earnings, both inventory risk (volatility is about to spike) and adverse selection (someone trading right before the announcement may well be informed) spike simultaneously, and the spread widens dramatically to compensate for both.
questions.professionalAnswer: This is really a question about which risk is the marginal driver in each regime. In a calm, liquid large-cap, the spread is mostly just covering the mechanical cost of doing business. Right before earnings in a thin name, it's almost entirely inventory and information risk — the operational cost barely changes, but the market maker is suddenly much more worried about both holding the position and who's on the other side of the trade.
questions.example: A liquid large-cap might trade with a one-cent spread dominated by exchange fees and technology cost; the same stock's spread could widen to several cents in the hour before its earnings release, driven almost entirely by spiking inventory risk and adverse selection rather than any change in operational cost.
commonMistakes: Describing all three components as equally important in every scenario
Not identifying which component specifically dominates in each named scenario
Treating 'volatility' as a single undifferentiated cause rather than tying it specifically to inventory risk
Missing that adverse selection is specifically about informed counterparties, not just general price uncertainty
keyPoints: Order-processing cost: largely fixed, dominates in calm, liquid conditions
Inventory risk: rises with volatility and uncertainty about holding the position
Adverse selection: rises when informed trading is more likely (e.g., pre-earnings)
Pre-earnings thin-name spreads widen due to inventory risk and adverse selection spiking together

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains all three spread components
Correctly identifies order-processing cost as dominant for the liquid large-cap case
Correctly identifies inventory risk and adverse selection as dominant for the pre-earnings thin-name case

questions.title: Stress Testing vs. VaR — When Each Is the Right Tool
questions.prompt: A risk committee wants to know both the typical-bad-day loss and what would happen if a 2008-style crisis recurred. Which tool answers which question, and why can't VaR alone answer both?
questions.modelAnswer: VaR and Expected Shortfall are statistical risk measures built from historical or modeled return distributions, answering 'how bad is a typical bad day, at a given confidence level.' They're only as good as the data and assumptions feeding them, and real markets occasionally do things that fall outside any recent statistical pattern. Stress testing answers a different question: historical scenario replay takes a real past crisis's actual market moves and asks what would happen to today's portfolio if those exact moves recurred — powerful because the scenario is historically grounded and internally consistent, but backward-looking by construction, since it can only replay crises that have already occurred. VaR alone can't answer the 2008-replay question because a statistical VaR model calibrated on recent, calmer data has no mechanism for capturing a genuinely unprecedented or historically extreme combined market move the way a direct scenario replay does.
questions.professionalAnswer: VaR is built from the statistics of 'normal-ish' history; a 2008 replay is explicitly asking what happens outside that normal range, using the actual moves that really happened rather than a distributional assumption. I'd tell the committee: VaR for the routine question, a named historical stress scenario for the crisis question — they're genuinely different tools built to answer different questions, not two ways of asking the same thing.
questions.example: A VaR model calibrated on the last two calm years might show a modest 1-day loss threshold, while a direct replay of the actual 2008 crisis's equity, credit-spread, and volatility moves against today's portfolio could reveal a far larger loss that the calm-period VaR model would never have surfaced on its own.
commonMistakes: Treating VaR as sufficient to answer both questions
Not explaining why VaR is backward-looking in a different, more limited way than a direct historical scenario replay
Confusing historical scenario replay with hypothetical/constructed scenarios
Missing that stress testing is explicitly designed to probe cases outside the recent statistical pattern VaR is built from
keyPoints: VaR/ES answer 'how bad is a typical bad day,' from recent historical/modeled statistics
Historical scenario replay directly re-applies a real past crisis's moves to today's portfolio
VaR alone can miss genuinely unprecedented or historically extreme combined moves
Stress testing and VaR are complementary tools answering different questions

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly distinguishes what VaR measures from what historical scenario replay measures
Explains why VaR alone can't answer the crisis-replay question
Frames the two tools as complementary, not substitutes

questions.title: Decomposing Expected Credit Loss
questions.prompt: A counterparty has a 3% probability of defaulting over the next year, a loss-given-default of 60%, and an exposure at default of $10 million. What's the expected credit loss, and why are the three inputs estimated separately rather than as one combined number?
questions.code: Expected credit loss ≈ PD x LGD x EAD
questions.modelAnswer: Expected credit loss ≈ PD x LGD x EAD = 0.03 x 0.60 x $10,000,000 = $180,000. The three components are estimated separately because they respond to fundamentally different drivers: probability of default (PD) largely reflects the counterparty's own creditworthiness and business risk, while loss given default (LGD) depends heavily on collateral, seniority, and bankruptcy recovery structure — a well-collateralized senior claim can have a much lower LGD than an unsecured junior one, even against the identical counterparty with the identical PD. Exposure at default (EAD) is the amount actually owed at the moment of default, which can itself vary with how the exposure is structured (e.g., a revolving credit line might have a different EAD than a fixed loan). Estimating them separately lets a risk team isolate and manage each driver independently, rather than being stuck with one opaque blended number.
questions.professionalAnswer: PD times LGD times EAD gives $180,000 here — straightforward multiplication once you have the three inputs. The reason they're not estimated as one lump figure is that each one is actionable in a different way: you manage PD through counterparty selection and credit limits, LGD through collateral and seniority structuring, and EAD through how the exposure itself is sized and structured — collapsing them into one number would hide which lever actually matters most for a given relationship.
questions.example: 0.03 x 0.60 x 10,000,000 = 180,000 — expected credit loss of $180,000 for this counterparty exposure.
commonMistakes: Multiplying the three numbers incorrectly or in the wrong units (e.g., forgetting to convert percentages to decimals)
Treating expected credit loss as the worst-case loss rather than the average expected loss
Not explaining why the three components are estimated and managed separately
Confusing LGD with PD (loss severity vs. likelihood of default)
keyPoints: Expected credit loss ≈ PD x LGD x EAD
PD reflects counterparty creditworthiness; LGD reflects collateral/seniority; EAD reflects amount owed at default
Separating the three lets a risk team manage each driver with a different, specific lever

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly computes the expected credit loss ($180,000)
Correctly explains what each of PD, LGD, and EAD represents
Explains why the three are estimated and managed separately

questions.title: Why Normal-Distribution VaR Understates Real Risk
questions.prompt: A risk model assumes daily returns are normally distributed and computes VaR from that assumption. What specific, well-documented statistical patterns in real financial returns make that assumption dangerous, and in which direction does the error typically point?
questions.modelAnswer: Real financial returns reliably show several patterns a normal distribution doesn't capture: fat tails (excess kurtosis above the normal's value of 3), meaning extreme moves happen far more often than a normal model predicts; volatility clustering, meaning large moves tend to be followed by more large moves rather than volatility staying constant; and negative skew via the leverage effect, meaning large down moves are typically more extreme than large up moves of equal probability. Because of fat tails specifically, a normal-distribution VaR model systematically understates the true probability and severity of extreme losses — the error points in the dangerous direction, making tail risk look smaller than it actually is, precisely in the scenarios where an accurate risk number matters most.
questions.professionalAnswer: The named stylized facts — fat tails, volatility clustering, negative skew from the leverage effect — all point the same direction: a normal-distribution VaR model is too optimistic about the tails specifically, which is exactly the part of the distribution you most need the model to get right. I'd want to see either a fat-tailed distribution (Student's t) used instead, or VaR calibrated via historical or Monte Carlo simulation rather than relying on normality.
questions.example: A normal model might predict that a 5-standard-deviation daily move should happen roughly once every few thousand years, while real market history shows such moves occurring far more frequently — exactly the gap fat tails describe.
commonMistakes: Naming only one stylized fact (usually fat tails) and missing the others
Not stating clearly which direction the resulting error points (understating risk, not overstating it)
Confusing excess kurtosis with skewness
Not proposing any alternative (fat-tailed distribution, historical/Monte Carlo VaR) to address the problem
keyPoints: Fat tails: extreme moves happen more often than a normal distribution predicts
Volatility clustering: large moves cluster, violating the constant-variance assumption
Negative skew / leverage effect: down moves tend to be more extreme than up moves
Normal-distribution VaR systematically understates true tail risk

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly names at least two of the relevant stylized facts
Correctly states the error direction (risk is understated, not overstated)
Proposes a reasonable alternative or mitigation

questions.title: Quick Continuous-Kelly Sizing
questions.prompt: A strategy has an annualized expected return of 12% and an annualized return variance of 0.04 (i.e., annualized volatility of 20%). Using the continuous Kelly formula, what fraction of capital should be allocated?
questions.modelAnswer: f* = mu / sigma^2 = 0.12 / 0.04 = 3.0, meaning full Kelly would allocate 300% of capital (3x leverage) to this strategy. That's an extreme sizing recommendation from the raw formula, and in practice this is exactly the kind of result that should trigger using fractional Kelly — commonly 25-50% of the full Kelly fraction — both because full Kelly is extremely volatile in practice and because mu is a noisy estimate with real sampling error that the formula has no way to account for on its own.
questions.professionalAnswer: 0.12 divided by 0.04 is 3 — that's the full Kelly answer, and it should immediately raise a flag rather than be taken at face value. A 300%-of-capital allocation from a single point estimate of mu is exactly the scenario fractional Kelly exists for, since an overestimated mu plugged into this formula produces an oversized position with no warning built into the math itself.
questions.example: f* = 0.12 / 0.04 = 3.0; a half-Kelly practitioner would instead size the position at 1.5x capital, and a quarter-Kelly practitioner at 0.75x — both dramatically more conservative than the raw full-Kelly output.
commonMistakes: Using the discrete Kelly formula instead of the continuous mu/sigma^2 form for a continuous-return strategy
Forgetting to square sigma, or using volatility (0.20) instead of variance (0.04) in the denominator
Treating the raw full-Kelly output as the actual recommended position size without caveat
Not flagging the sampling-error problem in the underlying mu estimate
keyPoints: Continuous Kelly: f* = mu / sigma^2
0.12 / 0.04 = 3.0 (300% of capital, i.e., 3x leverage)
Full Kelly is rarely used as-is due to volatility and estimation-error risk
Fractional Kelly (commonly 0.25-0.5x the full fraction) is the practical default

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Computes the correct full-Kelly fraction (3.0)
Uses the correct formula (variance, not volatility, in the denominator)
Flags the practical concern about using the raw result (fractional Kelly, estimation error)

questions.title: Quick Multi-Contract Delta-Hedge Rebalance
questions.prompt: You're short 50 call contracts (100 shares each), currently hedged with 2,200 long shares. The option's delta just moved from 0.44 to 0.52. How many additional shares do you need to buy or sell to restay hedged?
questions.modelAnswer: New required hedge = 50 contracts x 100 shares x 0.52 delta = 2,600 shares. Current hedge is 2,200 shares, so an additional 2,600 - 2,200 = 400 shares need to be bought to restore the hedge, since delta rose and the short-call position is now more negative-delta-exposed than before.
questions.professionalAnswer: New target is 50 x 100 x 0.52 = 2,600; current is 2,200; the gap is 400 shares to buy. The direction check is automatic once you remember that rising delta on a short call means more exposure to hedge, not less — so the adjustment has to add to the existing long stock hedge, not subtract from it.
questions.example: 50 x 100 x 0.52 = 2,600 target shares; 2,600 - 2,200 = 400 additional shares to buy.
commonMistakes: Computing the new hedge total correctly but then subtracting in the wrong direction
Forgetting the 100-share contract multiplier in the recalculation
Treating this as a one-time hedge rather than part of an ongoing rebalancing process
Confusing the direction (buy more vs. sell some) based on whether delta rose or fell
keyPoints: New hedge target = contracts x multiplier x current delta
New target: 50 x 100 x 0.52 = 2,600 shares
Additional shares needed = new target - current hedge = 400 to buy
Rising delta on a short-call position means more shares are needed, not fewer

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Computes the correct new target hedge (2,600 shares)
Computes the correct adjustment amount (400 shares)
Gets the direction (buy, not sell) correct

questions.title: Quick Portfolio Parametric VaR
questions.prompt: A $5 million portfolio has an annualized expected return of 8% and annualized volatility of 18%. Approximate the 1-day 99% VaR in dollar terms, using 252 trading days a year and z=2.33.
questions.code:
daily_sigma = annual_sigma / sqrt(252)
VaR = z * daily_sigma * portfolio_value (mu negligible at daily horizon)
questions.modelAnswer: Daily volatility ≈ 18% / sqrt(252) ≈ 18% / 15.87 ≈ 1.134%. Daily mean return (8%/252 ≈ 0.032%) is small enough to treat as roughly negligible at this horizon for a quick estimate. VaR_99 ≈ 2.33 x 1.134% ≈ 2.64% of portfolio value, or about 2.64% x $5,000,000 ≈ $132,000. This is a parametric approximation assuming normal returns — real daily returns have fatter tails, so this should be treated as a lower bound on true tail risk, not a precise ceiling.
questions.professionalAnswer: First step is always converting annual vol to daily by dividing by sqrt(252), which gives about 1.13%. Multiply by the 99% z-score of 2.33 to get roughly 2.64% of the portfolio, then apply that percentage to the $5 million — about $132,000. I'd flag immediately that this is a normal-distribution approximation and real tail risk is probably somewhat worse.
commonMistakes: Forgetting to convert annualized volatility to daily volatility before applying the z-score
Using the wrong z-score for the requested confidence level
Reporting the answer only as a percentage without converting to the requested dollar figure
Not flagging that this parametric/normal approximation likely understates true tail risk
keyPoints: Daily volatility = annual volatility / sqrt(252)
VaR_99 ≈ z_0.99 x daily_sigma, z ≈ 2.33
Result: roughly 2.64% of portfolio value, or about $132,000 on $5 million
This is a normal-distribution approximation, likely a lower bound on real tail risk

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly converts annual volatility to daily volatility
Computes a VaR dollar figure close to $132,000
Notes the normal-distribution approximation caveat

questions.title: Quick Hedge Ratio Calculation
questions.prompt: A strategy's daily returns have a covariance with the market's daily returns of 0.00018, and the market's daily return variance is 0.00012. What's the hedge ratio (beta), and what does it tell you about sizing a hedge against market exposure?
questions.modelAnswer: Beta = Cov(r_s, r_m) / Var(r_m) = 0.00018 / 0.00012 = 1.5. A beta of 1.5 means the strategy's returns move, on average, 1.5x as much as the market's — to hedge out that market exposure, a trader would need to short the equivalent of 1.5x the strategy's notional value in the market index (or an appropriate proxy), not a 1:1 hedge.
questions.professionalAnswer: 0.00018 divided by 0.00012 is 1.5 — clean division once the numbers are set up correctly. The practical consequence is that a naive 1:1 hedge would meaningfully under-hedge this position; the correct hedge notional is 1.5x the position being hedged, not an equal amount.

questions.title: Quick Coupon-Collector-Style Estimate
questions.prompt: A trader randomly samples stocks, one at a time with replacement, from a universe of 4 sectors, trying to see at least one stock from every sector. On average, how many draws will it take to see all 4 sectors at least once?

The logic: the first new sector takes 1 draw trivially, then each subsequent new sector is a geometric waiting time with success probability k/4 for the k-th remaining sector, and summing those geometric expectations (6/k become 4/k scaled for this n) gives the total.

The key insight worth stating out loud is that it's a sum of separate geometric waiting times, each one getting harder as fewer new sectors remain to be found.

questions.title: Diagnosing Worsening Adverse Selection
questions.prompt: A market maker notices their fills are increasingly 'wrong way' — right after they buy on the bid, the price tends to drop further than normal; right after they sell on the ask, it tends to rally further than normal. They suspect adverse selection has gotten worse. What's actually happening, and what general levers exist to respond, even without knowing the exact live quoting algorithm?
questions.modelAnswer: This pattern — fills that are systematically followed by the price continuing to move against the position just taken — is close to a textbook description of worsening adverse selection: more of the flow hitting the quotes is coming from counterparties with a genuine informational edge, so the market maker is losing more often and more severely to informed trading than the spread is currently compensating for. The standard responses, at a conceptual level, are to widen the spread (demanding more compensation per trade for the now-higher information risk), reduce the size offered at each price level (limiting how much can be picked off by an informed trader before the quote updates), and quote less aggressively or update quotes faster in response to new information, so the window during which a stale quote can be adversely selected shrinks.
questions.professionalAnswer: I can describe exactly what this pattern means and name the standard levers — wider spread, smaller size, faster quote updates — because those follow directly from the mechanics of what adverse selection is. What I'd be honest about is that the precise live algorithm for how much to widen, or exactly how to re-balance size versus speed in response to this specific signal, goes beyond what the foundational market-structure material covers — that's a genuine market-making engineering problem, and I'd want to be clear I'm reasoning from general principles rather than from a specific lesson on live quoting logic.
questions.example: A desk seeing this pattern consistently over several days might respond by widening its quoted spread by a few extra basis points and cutting the displayed size in half, rather than assuming the pattern is random noise and leaving the quote unchanged.

Overstating confidence about the precise live algorithm rather than being honest about the limits of general knowledge here

questions.title: The Kill Switch That Fired Too Late
questions.prompt: A strategy's daily loss limit was set at -$5,000. An investigation after a bad day shows the strategy actually lost $9,000 before the kill switch finally stopped new orders. The threshold logic itself was correct. What are the likely engineering causes of this delay, and how would you investigate?
questions.modelAnswer: If the threshold logic itself was correct but the switch fired late, the likely causes are in the plumbing around the check, not the check itself: the P&L or risk-check calculation might only run on a delayed cadence (e.g., once a minute or once per full bar, rather than after every fill), the order flow might have continued to be submitted and filled during the lag between the breach and the check actually running, or there could be a queueing/latency issue where the halt instruction itself took time to propagate and actually stop new orders from being accepted. Investigating this means examining the operational log — exactly when the breach actually occurred versus when the risk check last ran versus when the halt instruction was issued versus when the last new order was accepted — to pinpoint which of these gaps was actually responsible for the $4,000 of extra loss.
questions.professionalAnswer: The threshold being correct but the stop arriving $4,000 late points to latency somewhere in the pipeline, not the rule itself — either the check doesn't run often enough, or new orders kept being accepted in the gap between breach and halt actually taking effect. I'd go straight to the operational log and line up the exact timestamps of the breach, the check, the halt command, and the last accepted order, because that sequence will show exactly where the delay came from.
questions.example: If the risk check only runs once every 30 seconds rather than after every fill, a fast, sharp loss within one of those 30-second windows could breach the limit and keep trading for most of that window before the next scheduled check even notices.

questions.title: A Cross-Hedge That Isn't Working as Expected

What's the underlying problem, and is this a sign the hedge is broken?

questions.title: Inventory Keeps Building Even Though Quotes Look Symmetric
questions.prompt: A market maker's bid and ask are symmetric around their fair-value estimate, yet their inventory keeps drifting long day after day. If the quote itself isn't obviously mispriced, what else could be going on?
questions.modelAnswer: A symmetric quote around a fair-value estimate doesn't guarantee symmetric fills — if order flow itself is persistently one-sided (more natural sellers hitting the bid than natural buyers lifting the ask, for structural reasons like a broad market trend, a large persistent seller, or systematic rebalancing flow), inventory will drift in that direction even with a perfectly symmetric quote. The general concept that addresses this is quote skewing: deliberately shifting both sides of the quote (not just widening the spread) in the direction that discourages more of the flow that's been building inventory and encourages flow on the other side — in practice this is a genuine live market-making design problem that goes beyond foundational market-structure material, and the honest answer should be upfront about reasoning from general principles rather than a specific lesson on the live skewing algorithm.
questions.professionalAnswer: A symmetric quote assumes symmetric flow, and that assumption is exactly what's failing here — if sellers keep hitting the bid more than buyers lift the ask, the inventory drifts regardless of how fair the quote's center looks. Conceptually the fix is skewing the whole quote toward discouraging more of that flow, but I'd be upfront that the actual, real-time skewing algorithm is a market-making engineering problem that goes beyond what general market-structure knowledge covers in depth.
questions.example: If the fair value is $50.00 and the symmetric quote is 49.98/50.02, but sellers keep hitting the $49.98 bid far more than buyers lift the $50.02 ask, inventory grows long regardless of how centered the quote appears — the fix would be to skew the whole quote down, e.g. to 49.96/50.00, making the bid less attractive to sellers and the ask more attractive to buyers.

questions.title: Detecting Decay Before a Strategy Blows Up
questions.prompt: A strategy's whole-sample Sharpe ratio over three years still looks respectable at 1.1. But you suspect it's actually decaying. What specific diagnostic would reveal decay that the whole-period Sharpe is hiding, and what would you look for?
questions.modelAnswer: A single whole-period Sharpe ratio can hide a strategy that performed strongly for its first half and has been flat or negative for a while since, because the strong early period and the weak recent period simply average together into one respectable-looking number. The right diagnostic is a rolling-window Sharpe ratio — recomputing Sharpe over a moving window (e.g., six months), refreshed regularly, and plotting it over time. A real decay pattern shows up as a rolling Sharpe that starts strong and steadily declines toward zero or negative, even while the whole-period average still looks fine; a pre-committed rule flagging a review once the rolling Sharpe has stayed below a threshold for several consecutive checks (not just one, to avoid overreacting to short-term noise) is the standard way to act on this diagnostic systematically.
questions.professionalAnswer: A whole-period Sharpe of 1.1 can easily be hiding a strategy that was excellent for 18 months and dead for the last 18 — I wouldn't trust the single number without also looking at a rolling-window version of it. If the rolling Sharpe shows a steady decline toward zero over the back half of the sample, that's real decay the aggregate number was always going to mask.
questions.example: A strategy's rolling 6-month Sharpe might fall from 2.3 in the first half of a three-year sample to 0.2 in the back half, even though the whole-period average across all three years still computes to a respectable 1.1.

questions.title: Why a Dollar-Neutral Book Still Lost Money in a Panic
questions.prompt: A long/short equity book normally runs a beta to the market near 0.04 — essentially flat. During a sudden, broad market panic, that beta spiked to roughly 0.25, and the book lost money alongside the broader selloff despite being dollar-neutral. What happened, and does this mean dollar-neutral construction failed?
questions.modelAnswer: This is the correlation-to-one effect: when every sector sells off together in a panic, the diversification between the long leg and the short leg breaks down, because the two legs stop moving independently and instead start moving together in the same direction. Dollar-neutral construction reduces net market exposure on average, not in every regime — it's specifically during a broad, correlated panic that this protection is weakest, because that's exactly when cross-sectional diversification between longs and shorts collapses. This doesn't mean dollar-neutral construction 'failed' in some absolute sense; it means the honest, important caveat that 'dollar-neutral' is not a synonym for 'crisis-proof' was exactly right, and a book like this can still meaningfully outperform a long-only benchmark during such a crisis even while posting an uncomfortable absolute loss itself.

I wouldn't call this a failure of the construction; I'd call it the honest limit of what dollar-neutral actually promises, which is exactly the kind of nuance worth volunteering before being asked.

questions.title: A Dropped Acknowledgment Almost Doubled a Position
questions.prompt: A system submitted an order, the network call timed out before a response arrived, and the system automatically retried the exact same order. It turns out the original order had actually been accepted — the retry created a near-duplicate position before anyone noticed. Where did the design actually fail, and what's the fix?
questions.modelAnswer: The failure is the absence of idempotent order submission: the retry should have carried the exact same client order ID as the original attempt, which the broker (or an internal order management layer) would recognize as a duplicate and refuse to act on a second time. Without that de-duplication key, a retry after a dropped acknowledgment is indistinguishable from a genuinely new order, and the system has no way to know the original attempt actually succeeded. The fix is mechanical: every order submission must carry a unique client order ID, and any retry of the same logical order must reuse that same ID rather than generating a new one, so the broker's own de-duplication logic can catch the retry safely.
questions.professionalAnswer: This is a textbook idempotency gap — the retry logic exists, but it's generating what looks like a brand-new order instead of safely retrying the original one. The fix is specific and mechanical: attach a client order ID to every submission and reuse the exact same ID on any retry, so the broker's own de-duplication can catch it, rather than relying on the retry logic to somehow know the first attempt actually succeeded.
questions.example: A corrected retry would resubmit with client order ID 'algo-2024-001' a second time; the broker, recognizing that ID as already processed, would simply return the existing order's status instead of creating a second position.

questions.title: The Strategy That Stopped Scaling
questions.prompt: A strategy backtested beautifully at $500,000 of capital. Scaled up to $50 million, its net Sharpe dropped from 1.6 to 0.3. The signal logic didn't change. What happened, and how would you have caught this before deploying at the larger size?
questions.modelAnswer: This is a capacity problem: a backtest run only at a small, 'illustrative' position size never sees the cost of its own footprint, because a small order doesn't move the market. At $50 million, the same orders are now large enough relative to average daily volume that market impact — which scales roughly with the square root of the fraction of ADV traded — becomes a major, previously invisible cost, eating into the apparent edge. The way to catch this before deploying at scale is to explicitly estimate capacity ahead of time: model the strategy's gross edge, then model transaction costs and square-root market impact as a function of order size relative to ADV for the instruments actually traded, and find the capital level where that impact cost erodes the gross edge to roughly zero — that capacity ceiling should have been estimated and compared against the intended $50 million deployment size before committing to it.
questions.professionalAnswer: The signal didn't change, the market did — specifically, the cost of trading it at scale did. A strategy tested only at a small, convenient size never reveals its own capacity ceiling, because it never moves the market enough to see the impact. The fix is estimating capacity explicitly beforehand: model impact cost as a function of size relative to ADV, and find where it eats the edge to zero, rather than discovering the ceiling the expensive way by deploying past it.
questions.example: A strategy trading instruments where $500,000 represents a tiny fraction of daily volume might represent a 15-20% participation rate at $50 million — exactly the scale where square-root market impact stops being negligible and starts dominating the strategy's net returns.
commonMistakes: Assuming the signal itself must have broken, rather than recognizing a scale-dependent capacity problem
Not connecting this to the square-root market impact model and capacity concept specifically
Proposing no concrete method for estimating capacity ahead of time
Treating this as something that could only be discovered after the fact, rather than estimated in advance
keyPoints: A small-size backtest never reveals its own market impact, since a small order doesn't move the market
Market impact scales roughly with the square root of the participation rate (order size / ADV)
Capacity is the capital level where modeled impact cost erodes the gross edge to roughly zero
Capacity should be estimated explicitly before deploying at a larger size, not discovered after the fact

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses this as a market-impact/capacity problem, not a broken signal
Correctly describes the square-root impact relationship
Describes a concrete method for estimating capacity ahead of deployment

questions.title: A Signal Found by Testing a Thousand Variations
questions.prompt: A researcher tested roughly 1,000 parameter combinations against the same historical dataset and kept the one with the best Sharpe ratio, reporting it as the strategy's expected performance. What's wrong with reporting that number at face value, and what tool exists specifically to correct it?
questions.modelAnswer: Testing many strategy variations against the same historical dataset guarantees that some will show an impressively high Sharpe ratio purely by chance, even if every single variation tested is pure noise with zero real skill — this is data dredging / multiple-testing bias, and it's especially dangerous in finance because backtesting many parameter combinations is cheap and fast. Reporting the single best result from that search, at face value, systematically overstates the strategy's true expected future performance, because the selection process itself (picking the best of many) is part of what produced the impressive number, not the underlying edge alone. The deflated Sharpe ratio is the specific tool built to correct for this: it adjusts a strategy's Sharpe ratio downward based on how many trials were used to find it, giving a more honest estimate of whether the measured outperformance is likely to reflect real skill versus the expected best result of searching that many variations.
questions.professionalAnswer: With 1,000 variations tested against the same data, some will look great purely from chance — that's a near-certainty, not a surprise, even if none of them have any real edge. The deflated Sharpe ratio exists exactly for this situation: it takes the number of trials into account and tells you how much of that headline Sharpe should actually survive once you account for how much searching it took to find it.
questions.example: Simulating 1,000 strategies that are all pure noise with zero skill routinely produces a 'best' Sharpe ratio of 1.5-2.0 purely by chance — a number that looks like a genuine edge but reflects nothing more than the statistics of searching across many trials.
commonMistakes: Reporting the single best result from a large search as if it were an unbiased estimate of future performance
Not naming multiple testing / data dredging as the specific mechanism at work
Not naming the deflated Sharpe ratio as the tool built to correct for it
Treating a large number of tested variations as evidence of thoroughness rather than a source of statistical bias
keyPoints: Testing many variations against the same data guarantees some will look good by chance alone
This is multiple testing / data dredging bias, and it's cheap and easy to fall into with backtesting
Reporting only the best result overstates true expected future performance
The deflated Sharpe ratio adjusts for the number of trials used to find the strategy

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains why reporting the best of many trials is misleading
Names multiple testing / data dredging specifically
Names the deflated Sharpe ratio as the correcting tool

questions.title: Paper Trading Drifted From the Backtest — Now What?
questions.prompt: Three months of paper trading shows a correlation of 0.96 with the original backtest's predicted daily returns, but a cumulative return gap of -1.5 percentage points below what the backtest predicted over that period. Is this a reason to abandon the strategy before going live?
questions.modelAnswer: A correlation of 0.96 is reassuring — the paper-traded strategy is clearly tracking what the backtest expected it to do, day by day, rather than behaving like an unrelated process, so this isn't evidence the underlying signal is broken. The negative cumulative gap quantifies real-world friction (execution delay, slightly worse fills, data quirks) that even a careful backtest couldn't fully anticipate because some of it only shows up once the pipeline is actually running live — this is exactly the signal paper trading is designed to surface, not a reason for alarm on its own. The sensible next step is to understand what's driving the roughly 1.5-point gap specifically (is it consistent with a plausible friction cost, or does it suggest something structurally wrong) rather than treating either the high correlation or the negative gap in isolation as a final verdict.
questions.professionalAnswer: High correlation plus a modest negative gap is close to the expected, healthy outcome of a paper-trading period — it's telling you the signal is sound and real-world friction cost a little more than the backtest assumed. That's useful information to feed back into the cost model, not a reason to scrap the strategy; I'd want to understand whether the gap's size is consistent with known friction before concluding anything more serious is wrong.
questions.example: If the backtest assumed 5bps of round-trip cost and the realized paper-trading gap is consistent with an actual cost closer to 8-10bps, that's a useful, explainable correction to feed back into the cost assumptions rather than a sign the signal itself has failed.
commonMistakes: Treating any negative gap versus the backtest as proof the strategy should be abandoned
Ignoring the gap entirely because the correlation looks reassuring
Not proposing to investigate what specifically is driving the gap (friction cost vs. a structural problem)
Missing that high correlation and a modest negative gap together is close to the expected, healthy outcome of paper trading
keyPoints: High correlation indicates the signal is behaving as expected, day by day
A modest negative cumulative gap typically reflects real-world friction the backtest couldn't fully anticipate
This combination is close to a healthy, expected paper-trading outcome, not a red flag on its own
The right next step is investigating what's driving the specific size of the gap

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly interprets the high correlation as reassuring
Correctly interprets the gap as likely reflecting real friction, not a broken signal
Proposes investigating the gap's specific cause rather than reacting to either number in isolation

questions.title: TWAP, VWAP, or POV — Choosing an Execution Algorithm
questions.prompt: A desk needs to execute a large order and is deciding between TWAP, VWAP, and POV execution. Walk through the structural tradeoff each one makes, and describe a scenario where each would be the preferred choice.
questions.modelAnswer: TWAP splits the order into equal-sized pieces at equal time intervals, ignoring volume entirely — simple and predictable, but it trades the same size during naturally thin periods as during heavy ones, making its slices proportionally larger relative to available liquidity exactly when liquidity is scarcest; it's preferable when the trader wants a simple, predictable completion schedule and doesn't have (or trust) a reliable volume forecast. VWAP sizes each slice proportional to expected trading volume, participating more when the market is naturally busiest; it's preferable when a reliable volume-curve estimate exists and the goal is tracking the market's natural volume pattern closely. POV (percentage of volume) adapts in real time, continuously targeting a fixed fraction of whatever volume is actually printing right now, speeding up in active markets and slowing down in quiet ones; it's preferable when real-time responsiveness to actual, not predicted, market activity matters more than a fixed completion time — at the cost of an uncertain completion time if the market goes quiet.
questions.professionalAnswer: The core tradeoff across all three is predictability versus responsiveness. TWAP is the simplest and most predictable but blind to real conditions. VWAP is smarter, using a volume forecast, but is still following a pre-set curve rather than reacting live. POV is the most adaptive — reacting to real-time volume — at the cost of not knowing exactly when the order will finish. I'd reach for TWAP when I just need a simple, predictable schedule, VWAP when I trust the day's expected volume shape, and POV when real-time responsiveness matters more than a fixed completion time.
questions.example: A desk executing a routine rebalance with no urgency might default to VWAP against a typical U-shaped volume curve; a desk reacting to a fast-moving news event might prefer POV so execution speeds up automatically if volume surges, rather than being locked into a pre-set VWAP curve calibrated on a normal day.
commonMistakes: Describing TWAP and VWAP as functionally identical
Not identifying POV's real-time adaptiveness as its distinguishing structural feature
Missing the tradeoff each algorithm makes (predictability vs. responsiveness vs. forecast dependency)
Not giving a concrete scenario where each algorithm would actually be preferred
keyPoints: TWAP: equal time slices, simple, ignores real liquidity conditions
VWAP: slices sized to a volume forecast, tracks the market's natural volume curve
POV: real-time adaptive, targets a fixed fraction of live volume, uncertain completion time
Each makes a different tradeoff between predictability, forecast dependency, and real-time responsiveness

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly describes the structural mechanics of all three algorithms
Correctly articulates the predictability-vs-responsiveness tradeoff
Gives a sensible scenario for preferring each one

questions.title: Designing a Real-Time Risk Enforcement System
questions.prompt: Describe, at an architectural level, how a risk system should be designed to enforce hard limits (like a daily loss limit) in real time. What has to run continuously, and what has to happen automatically once a breach occurs?
questions.modelAnswer: A real-time risk system needs hard limits expressed as code that runs on every single update — after every trade, every fill, or every market data tick — rather than a periodic human review. Each check compares the current measure (cumulative daily P&L, current drawdown, position size) against a pre-committed hard threshold, decided in advance precisely so nobody has to make a judgment call in the heat of a bad moment. Once a breach is detected, the system should automatically take a pre-defined action — typically halting new order submission immediately and often flattening existing positions — without waiting for human confirmation, since the entire point of a kill switch is removing the hesitation that makes losses worse in a real crisis. The system should also distinguish hard-limit breaches (which trigger the automatic kill switch) from softer anomalies (which should only generate an alert to a human), since auto-stopping on every minor anomaly causes its own problems.
questions.professionalAnswer: The architecture has three pieces: continuous evaluation of risk measures against every update, not a periodic batch job; pre-committed hard thresholds decided before any bad day, not negotiated during one; and an automatic, immediate action — halt and often flatten — the moment a hard threshold is actually breached, with no human-in-the-loop delay for that specific category of breach. The split between hard-limit kill-switch triggers and softer human-alert anomalies is just as important as the automation itself, since treating every anomaly the same way in either direction causes real problems.
questions.example: A well-designed system evaluates cumulative daily P&L after every single fill; the instant that figure crosses the pre-set -$10,000 limit, the system automatically stops accepting new orders and flattens open positions within the same evaluation cycle, with no human approval step required for that specific, pre-committed threshold.
commonMistakes: Describing a periodic (e.g., once-per-minute or once-daily) check rather than a continuous, update-driven one
Proposing a human-in-the-loop approval step for a hard-limit breach, defeating the purpose of a kill switch
Not distinguishing hard-limit automatic triggers from softer human-alert anomalies
Omitting the pre-commitment principle (deciding the threshold in advance, not in the moment)
keyPoints: Risk checks must be code running continuously on every update, not a periodic review
Thresholds must be pre-committed in advance, removing in-the-moment judgment calls
A hard-limit breach should trigger an automatic, immediate halt (and often flatten), with no human approval delay
Hard-limit kill-switch triggers must be distinguished from softer, human-alert anomalies

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly describes continuous, update-driven risk evaluation
Correctly describes automatic, immediate action on breach with no human delay
Distinguishes hard-limit kill-switch triggers from softer alerts

questions.title: FIX, REST, or Native API — Weighing the Tradeoffs
questions.prompt: A firm is deciding how to connect its trading system to a broker. Compare FIX, REST, and a native proprietary API across latency, complexity, and flexibility, and explain which one an institutional desk running latency-sensitive strategies would most likely choose and why.
questions.modelAnswer: REST APIs are simple to integrate, using HTTP requests with JSON responses, but typically carry higher latency and no persistent push connection, so a separate mechanism (WebSocket or polling) is usually needed to learn about fills as they happen — this makes REST most common for retail and less latency-sensitive institutional use. FIX (Financial Information eXchange) is a persistent, stateful session over which orders and execution reports flow as structured messages — lower latency and the de facto institutional standard, but materially more complex to implement correctly, requiring careful session management, sequence numbers, and message recovery after a disconnect. A native/proprietary API is often the easiest way to get started with one specific venue, wrapping one of the above with convenience methods, at the cost of vendor lock-in if a second broker or venue is ever needed. A latency-sensitive institutional desk would most likely choose FIX specifically because its persistent, stateful session structure minimizes the connection overhead on every single message, which matters enormously once speed itself is part of the strategy's edge — accepting the added implementation complexity as the necessary cost of that speed.
questions.professionalAnswer: REST is the easy-to-integrate, higher-latency option; FIX is the lower-latency, harder-to-implement institutional standard; a native API is a venue-specific shortcut with lock-in risk. For a latency-sensitive desk, FIX is the obvious choice despite the added complexity, because the persistent session avoids re-establishing connection overhead on every message — exactly the kind of overhead a strategy where speed matters can't afford to pay repeatedly.
questions.example: A desk running a strategy where microseconds matter would accept the real engineering cost of building and maintaining proper FIX session management — sequence numbers, reconnection/recovery logic — rather than accept REST's simpler integration at the cost of materially higher per-message latency.
commonMistakes: Recommending REST for a latency-sensitive institutional strategy without acknowledging its latency disadvantage
Not naming the specific tradeoffs (latency, complexity, flexibility/lock-in) for each option
Describing FIX as simple to implement, understating its real session-management complexity
Not committing to a clear recommendation with sound reasoning for the latency-sensitive scenario
keyPoints: REST: simple integration, higher latency, needs a separate mechanism for real-time fill updates
FIX: lower latency, persistent stateful session, materially more complex to implement correctly
Native API: easiest for one specific venue, at the cost of lock-in
A latency-sensitive institutional desk would typically choose FIX, accepting complexity for speed

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly compares all three options across latency, complexity, and flexibility
Makes a clear, well-reasoned recommendation for the latency-sensitive scenario
Acknowledges the real implementation cost of the recommended option

questions.title: Designing Risk Budgeting Across a Portfolio
questions.prompt: A portfolio holds several positions with different sizes, volatilities, and correlations. Describe how you'd architect a risk-budgeting process that allocates risk deliberately rather than just allocating equal dollar amounts.
questions.code:
portfolio_vol = sqrt(w' * Sigma * w)
marginal_contrib = (Sigma @ w) / portfolio_vol
risk_contrib = w * marginal_contrib
questions.modelAnswer: The architecture needs a covariance matrix (Sigma) of asset returns, updated regularly, combined with the current position weights (w) to compute total portfolio volatility as sqrt(w'Sigma w). From there, each position's marginal contribution to risk is (Sigma @ w) / portfolio_vol, and its actual risk contribution is w_i times its marginal contribution — these risk contributions sum exactly to total portfolio volatility, giving a clean decomposition of where risk is actually concentrated. The deliberate risk-budgeting step is comparing each position's risk_contrib_pct against an intended target allocation (not necessarily equal dollar weights) and resizing positions so dollar weights match the intended risk allocation, rather than treating equal dollar amounts as automatically fair — a volatile or highly correlated position can dominate portfolio risk despite a modest dollar weight if this check isn't performed.
questions.professionalAnswer: The core architecture is: maintain a live covariance matrix, compute each position's marginal and total risk contribution from it, and then size dollar positions to match an intentional risk target rather than an intentional dollar target. The thing this catches that equal-dollar-weighting misses completely is a volatile or highly correlated position quietly dominating total portfolio risk while looking perfectly reasonable on a dollar-weight basis alone.
questions.example: Two positions with equal $1 million dollar weights could have very different risk contributions if one has three times the volatility of the other — a risk-budgeting system would flag this and resize the dollar weights so each position's actual contribution to total portfolio risk matches the intended allocation, rather than leaving both at an equal dollar amount.
commonMistakes: Describing risk budgeting as equivalent to equal-dollar-weighting
Omitting the covariance matrix as the necessary input for computing true risk contributions
Not explaining the marginal-contribution-to-risk calculation correctly
Missing that risk contributions, by construction, sum exactly to total portfolio volatility
keyPoints: Requires a covariance matrix of asset returns as the core input
Portfolio volatility = sqrt(w'Sigma w); marginal contribution = (Sigma w)/portfolio_vol
Risk contribution per position = weight x its marginal contribution, summing to total volatility
Risk budgeting resizes dollar weights to match an intentional risk allocation, not an equal-dollar default

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly describes the covariance-based risk contribution calculation
Correctly explains why equal dollar weights don't imply equal risk contributions
Describes resizing positions to match an intentional risk target as the actual budgeting step

questions.title: What a Market-Making Engine Has to Track
questions.prompt: Conceptually, what does a market-making engine need to track and update continuously in order to quote intelligently, beyond just 'a bid and an ask'? Be honest about where your answer draws on general industry knowledge versus specific course material.
questions.modelAnswer: At minimum, a market-making engine needs to track current inventory (position size and direction, continuously updated with every fill), a fair-value estimate for the instrument being quoted (updated as new information arrives), the current spread being charged relative to that fair value (reflecting order-processing cost, inventory risk, and adverse-selection risk), and some measure of recent fill patterns or flow toxicity to detect when adverse selection is worsening. From there, inventory and estimated risk feed into how the quote should be skewed away from fair value in the direction that discourages further unwanted inventory buildup. This is the general shape of the problem that follows directly from why the spread exists in the first place — but the specific live algorithms for fair-value estimation, flow-toxicity detection, and quote-skewing in a real production engine are a deeper, specialized market-making engineering problem than the foundational market-structure material in this course covers in detail, and I'd want to be clear that's where general industry knowledge is doing the work, not a specific lesson's content.
questions.professionalAnswer: I can lay out the shape of what has to be tracked — inventory, a fair-value estimate, the current spread relative to that fair value, and some read on flow quality — because all four follow directly from the mechanics of why a spread exists at all. What I'd be upfront about is that this course's foundational material explains those mechanics clearly but doesn't walk through the actual production algorithms for live fair-value estimation or flow-toxicity scoring — that's genuinely deeper, specialized engineering knowledge I'm drawing from general industry understanding rather than a specific lesson.
questions.example: A simplified engine might track: current inventory of +2,000 shares, a fair-value estimate of $50.02 updated from recent trade prints, a quoted spread of 49.99/50.05 already skewed down slightly because of the long inventory, and a rolling measure of how often recent fills have been immediately followed by adverse price moves.
commonMistakes: Describing only 'a bid and an ask' without the underlying state (inventory, fair value, flow quality) that drives them
Overstating confidence about the exact live production algorithm as if it were covered in specific course material
Not connecting the tracked state back to the three spread components (processing cost, inventory risk, adverse selection)
Failing to be honest about the boundary between general knowledge and specific lesson content

These four pieces follow directly from the mechanics of why a spread exists
Inventory and risk estimates drive how the quote should be skewed

questions.title: Building a Point-in-Time Universe
questions.prompt: A backtest currently builds its tradable universe from 'today's S&P 500 constituents' and applies that same list to every historical date. Describe architecturally how a point-in-time universe should actually be constructed, and what data this requires that a simple current-constituent list doesn't provide.
questions.modelAnswer: A point-in-time universe requires a historical record of index membership changes — exactly which instruments were actual members of the relevant index as of each specific historical date, including every instrument that was later removed due to delisting, bankruptcy, or acquisition. Architecturally, instead of fetching a single current-constituent list and applying it to the entire backtest period, the system needs a function that, given any historical date, returns the membership as it actually stood on that date — `get_universe(date)` called fresh for each simulated date in the backtest loop, rather than computed once outside the loop. This is harder to obtain than a current list (many free data sources only provide today's membership), but it's essential for any backtest making claims about trading a broad universe rather than a single still-existing instrument, since using today's survivors applied retroactively silently excludes every historical failure and inflates the measured return of nearly any strategy trading that universe.
questions.professionalAnswer: The fix is structural, not just a data source swap: the universe-lookup has to be a function of the simulated date, called inside the backtest loop for every date, rather than a single list fetched once outside it. That requires actual historical membership-change data — additions and removals with their effective dates — which is a genuinely harder dataset to source than 'today's constituents,' but there's no way around needing it if the backtest is going to make an honest claim about a broad, historically evolving universe.
questions.example: A stock that was added to the index in 2019 and one that was removed in 2016 for underperformance should both be correctly reflected in a 2015 backtest date's universe — present or absent exactly as they actually were at that point in history, not according to today's list.
commonMistakes: Proposing to simply 'use better data' without describing the structural function-of-date change needed
Not recognizing that the universe lookup must be called inside the backtest's date loop, not once outside it
Missing that this specifically requires historical addition/removal data with effective dates, not just a current snapshot
Not connecting this back to why survivorship bias inflates backtested returns
keyPoints: Point-in-time universe requires historical membership-change data (additions/removals with effective dates)
The universe lookup must be a function of the simulated date, called per-date inside the backtest loop
This data is harder to source than a current-constituent snapshot
Using today's survivors retroactively silently excludes historical failures, inflating measured returns

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly describes the structural, per-date universe lookup design
Correctly identifies the specific historical membership data required

questions.title: Designing the Operational Log
questions.prompt: Design the contents of an operational log for a live trading strategy. What specifically should it record, and why does recording every risk check (not just breaches) matter?
questions.modelAnswer: A production strategy's operational log should record every order submitted (with its client order ID), every fill with its actual execution price, every risk-limit check performed and its result — not just the breaches — and every alert or kill-switch trigger with a precise timestamp. Logging only breaches, and not every check, means there's no record of the system's normal operation to compare against when something does go wrong — you can't tell whether a risk check simply didn't run during a bad window versus ran and correctly found no breach, which is exactly the ambiguity that makes a delayed kill-switch incident (checks ran too infrequently? didn't run at all?) impossible to diagnose after the fact. A complete log turns 'the strategy lost money last Tuesday, not sure why' into an answerable question by letting someone reconstruct exactly what happened, in what order, after the fact.
questions.professionalAnswer: The non-obvious design choice is logging every check, not just the breaches — without that, you can't distinguish 'the risk check ran and correctly passed' from 'the risk check simply never ran during that window,' and those are two very different incidents with very different fixes. The log's entire value is in letting someone reconstruct the exact sequence of events after the fact, which requires recording the boring, uneventful checks just as rigorously as the dramatic ones.
questions.example: If an incident investigation finds a gap of several minutes with no risk-check log entries at all during the exact window a loss limit was breached, that immediately points to the check simply not running during that window — a finding that would be invisible if only breaches, and not every check, had been logged.

Not explaining why logging only the exceptional events makes incident diagnosis ambiguous
Omitting client order IDs or precise timestamps from the proposed log design
Treating the log as only useful for after-the-fact storytelling rather than active incident diagnosis
